title: Life began in water: from the first tiny cells to us

summary.text: Dry baking soda and dry citric acid can sit side by side for months, and nothing happens. Add a few drops of water, and they fizz at once. Water lets chemicals move about, meet and change. That is why life began in water, more than 3.5 billion years ago. The first living beings were tiny cells in the sea, far too small to see. Very slowly, over a very long time, they became every kind of living being on Earth, including you.
summary.art: A steel katori of white powder fizzing with bubbles where a few drops of water have landed, beside a dry katori where nothing happens.

intro.hook: Put a pinch of baking soda and a pinch of citric acid side by side on a dry steel plate. Push them together with a dry spoon. Watch for one minute. Is anything happening?
intro.text: Dry powders can sit together for months and stay just the same. Yet a few drops of water change them in a second. In this unit you find out what water does to them. Then you find out why every living being began in water, long ago, and how long the story of life really is. Before you read on, make a guess. Will the powders fizz if you pour cooking oil on them instead of water? You are going to test it.
intro.art: A girl kneeling at a kitchen counter, watching two small heaps of white powder on a steel plate, with a dry spoon in her hand.

outcomes: By the end I can say that baking soda and citric acid change only when water lets them meet.
By the end I can say that life began in water, and that every cell in my body is still mostly water.
By the end I can say that the first living beings were tiny cells, far too small to see.
By the end I can put the big steps in the story of life in order, from the first cells to humans.
By the end I can use the Year of Life calendar to show that life was tiny cells for most of the story.
By the end I can say that every living being today, including me, comes from the first cells, and that new kinds came very slowly.

terms.meaning: When two or more chemicals meet and change into new chemicals, we say they react.
terms.example: Baking soda and citric acid react in water and make bubbles of gas.
terms.art: Two small heaps of powder in a katori of water, with bubbles rising where they meet.

terms.meaning: To spread out into a liquid in pieces too small to see, the way sugar seems to vanish in tea.
terms.example: Water dissolves citric acid, so the citric acid can spread and meet the baking soda.
terms.art: A spoon of sugar disappearing as it is stirred into a steel tumbler of water.

terms.meaning: The smallest living unit of any living being. Some living beings are one cell. You are made of a huge number of cells.
terms.example: The first living beings on Earth were each one single cell, living in water.
terms.art: A round cell drawn large, with a thin skin around a watery inside, floating in blue water.

terms.meaning: The remains or the mark of a living being from long ago, kept in rock.
terms.example: A shell pressed into stone, or the layers a mat of tiny cells left behind, are fossils.
terms.art: A grey rock with the shape of a spiral shell pressed into it.

terms.meaning: A rock built up in thin layers by a mat of tiny cells living in shallow water. Sand sticks to the mat, and the cells grow up through it again and again.
terms.example: The oldest stromatolites we know are about 3.5 billion years old. Some still grow today, at Shark Bay in Australia.
terms.art: A cut rock showing wavy stacked layers, like the pages of a closed book bent into a dome.

terms.meaning: Anyone you come from: a parent, a grandparent, a great-grandparent, and on and on, back and back.
terms.example: Your great-grandmother is your ancestor. So, very far back, were tiny cells in the sea.
terms.art: A line of mothers, each one holding the hand of her own mother, fading back into a blue sea.

terms.meaning: A line that shows things in the order they happened, the oldest at one end and the newest at the other.
terms.example: The Year of Life calendar is a timeline of the story of life squeezed into one year.
terms.art: A long strip of paper with small pictures in a row: a hot planet, a sea, a fish, a dinosaur, a child.

terms.meaning: A thousand million. Written out, it is 1 followed by nine zeros: 1,000,000,000.
terms.example: The Earth is about four and a half billion years old.
terms.art: A huge heap of rice grains with a label saying one thousand million.

terms.meaning: A long, thin chain of chemicals inside every cell. RNA carries instructions, and some kinds of RNA can help make copies of other chains.
terms.example: Many scientists think the very first life may have used RNA to store its instructions.
terms.art: A long wavy chain of beads in four colours, floating in water.

explanations.concept: Why the powders fizzed only in water
explanations.context: This card explains the dry mix test, where baking soda and citric acid fizzed in water and sea water, but not dry or in oil.
explanations.definition: Two chemicals react when their tiny pieces meet. Baking soda and citric acid can only meet when water dissolves them.
explanations.description: A grain of dry powder is a solid. Its tiny pieces stay stuck in place, so the two powders hardly meet at all. Water dissolves the grains. Then their tiny pieces spread out through the water and bump into each other. When baking soda meets citric acid, they react and make a gas called carbon dioxide. That gas makes the bubbles. Oil does not dissolve these powders, so nothing happened in the oil bowl. As soon as you added water to the oil bowl, the powder fizzed. It had been ready all along.
examples: Fruit salt sits quietly in a dry packet, and fizzes in a tumbler of water.
Cooks in Gujarat add fruit salt or soda to wet dhokla batter, so it fills with bubbles and rises.
Sea water made the powders fizz just like tap water, because the sea is water too.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: dry grains of two powders sitting apart, and the same powders in water with their tiny pieces spread out and bubbles rising.

explanations.context: This card explains why scientists say life began in water, long ago.
explanations.definition: The chemicals of life move about, meet and react in water. So life began in water, more than 3.5 billion years ago, and every living being still needs water inside them.
explanations.description: Inside every living cell, the chemicals of life are dissolved in water, like the powders in your bowl. There they meet and react all day long. That is how a cell grows, uses food and makes copies of itself. So scientists think life could only begin where there was liquid water. The oldest clear signs of life come from rocks that formed in shallow sea water about 3.5 billion years ago, in Australia. In 2006, the Australian scientist Abigail Allwood and her team showed that some of these rocks are stromatolites, built by mats of tiny cells. Your own cells are mostly water too. More than half of your body is water.
examples: The oldest stromatolites formed in shallow sea water about 3.5 billion years ago.
A moong seed stays dry and still for months, and begins to grow only when water reaches the seed.
When people look for life on Mars, they look first for signs of water.
explanations.art: A shallow sea long ago, with low dome-shaped mats of tiny cells on the sea floor and a red rocky shore with nothing growing on it.

explanations.concept: Where in the water did life begin?
explanations.context: This card is about a question scientists still argue about: in which kind of water did the first life begin?
explanations.description: Scientists agree that life began in water. They do not agree on which water. Each idea has some evidence, and nobody has found the answer yet.
examples: Hot springs on the deep sea floor still pour out warm water full of chemicals.
Hot spring pools on land, in places like Iceland, dry out and fill up again.
Big craters made by rocks from space filled with water on the young Earth.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study the deep sea, such as Michael Russell and William Martin
perspectives.explanation: Life began at hot springs on the deep sea floor. There, warm water full of chemicals meets cold sea water, and rocks have tiny holes where chemicals can gather.

perspectives.who: Scientists who study hot springs on land, such as David Deamer and Bruce Damer
perspectives.explanation: Life began in warm pools on land that dried out and filled up again. Drying pushes chemicals close together, so they can join into long chains. Charles Darwin guessed something like this in 1871, when he wrote of a warm little pond.

perspectives.who: Sankar Chatterjee, a scientist born in India who works in the United States
perspectives.explanation: Life began in lakes inside craters made by rocks from space. The rocks brought chemicals, and the crater floors had hot springs.

explanations.art: Three small pictures: a dark deep sea floor with a smoking hot spring, a steaming pool on bare land, and a round crater lake.

explanations.concept: The first living beings were tiny cells
explanations.context: This card explains what the first living beings were like.
explanations.definition: A cell is the smallest living unit of any living being. The first living beings were each one single tiny cell.
explanations.description: The first living beings were far too small to see. Tiny cells today, like bacteria, are so small that about 50 of them, side by side, would just stretch across one hair. Scientists think the first cells were this tiny too. Each cell had a thin skin around a watery inside. Each cell took in food from the water, grew, and split in two to make more cells. Tiny cells like these sense food and swim towards it, and the first cells sensed their world too. They lived in mats and films on the sea floor. We know about them from stromatolites and from chemicals they left in old rocks. For nearly 3 billion years, almost all life on Earth was tiny cells like these.
examples: A green slimy film on a wet wall or in a rain puddle is made of tiny water-living cells.
Stromatolites at Shark Bay in Australia are still being built by mats of tiny cells today.
Your body is made of cells too, a huge number of them, each one mostly water.
explanations.art: A single hair drawn huge across the page, with a row of about 50 tiny round cells lying along its width.

explanations.concept: The RNA idea: how the first cell may have started
explanations.context: This card is about one idea of how the first living cell could have formed. Nobody knows for sure.
explanations.description: Every cell today keeps instructions in long chains called DNA and RNA. RNA can carry instructions, and some RNA can also help join chemicals together. So many scientists think the first life may have used RNA alone. A chain of RNA that could help make copies of itself would make more and more chains. If a bubble of fat closed around such chains, that bubble could have become the first cell. This is an idea, not a finding. Nobody has yet made a living cell from chemicals in a lab.
examples: In labs, scientists have made RNA chains that can join other small chains together.
Bubbles of fat form by themselves when some oily chemicals are shaken in water.
Every cell alive today still uses RNA to turn instructions into working parts.

perspectives.explanation: RNA came first. It can carry instructions and help make copies, so it could have done both jobs before DNA and the other parts of cells existed.
Cycles of chemical reactions came first, using energy from hot springs. Chains like RNA came later, once those reactions were running.

explanations.art: A soft round bubble of fat in water, with a few wavy chains of coloured beads floating inside.

explanations.context: This card explains how the first tiny cells became all the kinds of living beings, and how long that took.
explanations.definition: Every living being comes from parents, and they came from theirs, back to the first cells. Over a very long time, small changes added up, and a few kinds became many kinds.
explanations.description: Children are a little different from their parents. Over thousands and thousands of generations, these small differences add up. That is how new kinds of living beings come about. It is very slow. For most of life's story, all life was tiny cells in water. The first animals big enough to see appeared in the sea only about 575 million years ago. Plants grew onto land about 470 million years ago. Animals with four legs walked out of the water about 375 million years ago. Humans like us appeared only about 300,000 years ago, in Africa. The crow at your window, the coconut tree, the ant on the floor and you all come from those first cells. You are all very distant cousins.
examples: The first animals big enough to see were soft, flat and lived in the sea.
Birds come from dinosaurs, so the crow at your window is a living dinosaur.
Humans and monkeys are cousins: they come from the same ancestors, millions of years back.
explanations.art: A branching tree drawn from one small dot at the bottom, its branches ending in a fish, a coconut tree, a crow, an ant and a child.

agreed.evidence: The oldest signs of life are in rocks that formed in water. Every living being needs water inside their cells, where the chemicals of life meet and react.

agreed.text: The first life was tiny single cells, and for most of life's story almost all life was tiny cells.
agreed.evidence: The oldest fossils are stromatolites and tiny cells, about 3.5 billion years old. Fossils of animals big enough to see appear only about 575 million years ago.

agreed.text: The Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.
agreed.evidence: Radioactive rocks act like clocks. In 1956, Clair Patterson measured lead in meteorites and found the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old.

agreed.text: Every living being today comes from those first cells.
agreed.evidence: All living cells use the same kind of instructions, DNA and RNA, and build themselves from the same kinds of chemicals. Fossils in older and newer rocks show kinds changing over time.

challenging.claim: Life began in the deep sea.
challenging.who: Many scientists who study the sea
challenging.for: Hot springs on the deep sea floor pour out warm water full of the chemicals life needs, and their rocks have tiny holes where chemicals can gather.
challenging.against: Other scientists point out that long chains like RNA fall apart easily in lots of water. They think pools on land that dry and fill again suit life better.
challenging.context: This card is about where life began. Scientists agree it was in water, but not which water.

challenging.claim: Life came to Earth from space.
challenging.who: A few scientists, starting with the idea called panspermia
challenging.for: Some meteorites carry chemicals that living things use. A meteorite that fell in Murchison, Australia, in 1969 held amino acids, which are building blocks of life.
challenging.against: No living being has ever been found in a meteorite. And the idea only moves the question: how did life begin wherever it came from?
challenging.context: This card is about an unusual idea of where Earth's life came from.

challenging.for: Humans and monkeys have many things in common, such as hands that grip, eyes at the front and a similar skeleton.
challenging.against: Monkeys did not turn into humans. Humans and monkeys are cousins. They both come from the same ancestors, who lived millions of years ago and were neither of them.
challenging.context: This card is about a mistake many people make about where humans come from.

challenging.claim: The Earth and its life are only a few thousand years old.
challenging.who: An old idea, held by many people in the past
challenging.for: Long ago, people worked out the age of the world from family lists and old stories.
challenging.against: Rock clocks made by radioactivity show rocks billions of years old. Layers of rock and fossils took a very long time to build up.
challenging.context: This card is about how old people once thought the Earth was.

big_questions.q: The fruit salt in the packet waited for months without changing. Living seeds also wait for months, then grow. How is a waiting seed different from waiting powder?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to the powder and to the seed when water reaches them.

big_questions.q: If there had been no water on Earth, could life have begun at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about the dry bowl and the oil bowl in your test.

big_questions.q: Far enough back, your great-great-great-grandmother was a tiny cell in water. Is a part of her still in you?
big_questions.hint: Every one of your cells came from another cell. Think about where that chain goes back to.

big_questions.q: Humans arrived in the last half hour of the Year of Life. Does arriving last make us less important, more important, or neither?
big_questions.hint: Think about who lived on Earth before us, and who still lives here with us.

big_questions.q: Could new life begin today, from chemicals, in a pond or in the sea?
big_questions.hint: Charles Darwin wondered about this in 1871. Think about what the tiny cells living there now might do to any new chemicals.

how_we_found_out.context: How do we know how old the Earth is, and how long life has had to change? This card tells the true story.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, many people thought the Earth was only a few thousand years old. In 1862, the famous scientist Lord Kelvin worked out how long a hot young Earth would take to cool down. He said it was between 20 and 400 million years old. Later he said only about 20 to 40 million. Charles Darwin was worried. He thought the many kinds of life needed far longer than that to come about. Then, in 1896, Henri Becquerel found that uranium gives off rays. Marie Curie named this radioactivity. Radioactive rock slowly turns into other materials, at a steady speed, like a clock. It also makes heat inside the Earth, which Kelvin did not know about. So his cooling sum was wrong. In 1911, a young British geologist, Arthur Holmes, used this rock clock and found rocks about 1.6 billion years old. In 1956, the American scientist Clair Patterson measured lead in meteorites, rocks that fell from space. He found that the Earth is about 4.5 billion years old. Scientists still use that age today.
how_we_found_out.who: Lord Kelvin, Henri Becquerel, Marie Curie, Arthur Holmes and Clair Patterson
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That the Earth was young: first a few thousand years, then Kelvin's 20 to 40 million years. Kelvin did not know that radioactive rock heats the Earth. Rock clocks then showed rocks billions of years old, and Patterson's meteorites gave 4.5 billion years.
how_we_found_out.art: Marie Curie in her lab with glass bottles, and beside her a cut rock and a dark meteorite on a table, with a clock face drawn on the rock.

story.title: The Packet That Waited
story.note: Kavya, Arun and Paati are made up. Fruit salt is a fizzy powder sold at chemists, and it is mostly baking soda and citric acid. Chennai gets heavy rain from October to December.
text: It was raining hard in Chennai. Kavya, who was eight, and her little brother Arun, who was six, could not go down to play. Their grandmother, Paati, was in the kitchen, tidying the spice shelf.
Arun found a small packet at the back of the shelf. "What is this, Paati?"
"Fruit salt," said Paati. "Grown-ups stir it into water when their stomach feels sour. That packet has been sitting there since Deepavali."
Arun shook the packet. The powder inside made a soft rattle. "It's just white dust," he said.

"Watch this," said Kavya. She tipped a pinch of the powder into a steel tumbler of water. At once the water hissed and fizzed. Tiny bubbles jumped up to the top. Arun leaned in so close that the bubbles tickled his nose.
"So why didn't it fizz in the packet?" asked Arun. "It just sat there for months."
Kavya opened her mouth to answer. Then she shut it again. She did not know.
Paati smiled. "Let's find out. Fruit salt is mostly two powders mixed together, baking soda and citric acid. I have both in the kitchen." She put four steel katoris on the counter.

Kavya measured half a spoon of baking soda and half a spoon of citric acid into each katori. Arun stirred them with a dry spoon. Nothing happened. He put his ear right down by a katori and listened. Nothing.
"Now each bowl gets something different," said Paati. "Oil in this one, water in this one, sea water in this one. The last one stays dry."
"We don't have any sea water," said Arun.
Kavya stirred a spoon of salt into half a tumbler of water. She let Arun taste one drop from her fingertip. He screwed up his face. "That is about how salty the sea is," she told him.
"First, guess," said Paati. Arun was sure the oil would fizz most, because oil is thick and strong. Kavya thought only the plain water would fizz.

Kavya poured two spoons of oil into the first katori. The oil lay on the powder like a yellow blanket. Not one bubble came. She poured two spoons of water into the next one. It fizzed at once, loud and white. Then the sea water. It fizzed just as hard. The dry katori sat there, still and quiet.
"So the sea is still water," said Kavya. "The salt doesn't stop it."

Then Paati handed her the tumbler of plain water. "Try the oil bowl again." Kavya dripped water into the oil. The drops sank slowly through the yellow oil. The moment they touched the powder, bubbles came climbing up through the oil like a string of tiny beads.
"The powder in the oil was ready all along," said Kavya slowly. "It only needed water."

Paati nodded. "Dry powder is made of grains. In a grain, the tiny pieces stay stuck where they are. Water dissolves them. Then the tiny pieces can move about and meet. When baking soda meets citric acid, they react, and they make the gas in the bubbles."
Arun looked at the fizzing sea water bowl. "Did the sea fizz like this, long ago?"

Paati laughed. "Not like this. But something a bit like it happened, very slowly. Chemicals floated in the water. They met and changed, again and again. After a very long time, some of them became the first living cells. Each one was far too small to see. That is why life began in water."

She took last year's calendar down from the wall and turned it to January. "Let's pretend the whole story of the Earth is one year. On the first of January, the Earth forms, hot and rocky." She turned to March. "At the end of March, we find the first signs of tiny cells in the sea."
Arun turned the pages. April. May. June. July. "Where are the animals?"

"Keep turning," said Paati. August. September. October. Still tiny cells. At last, in the middle of November, came the first animals big enough to see, soft and flat, on the sea floor. Then everything rushed into the last weeks of the year: plants and animals on land, dinosaurs, and flowers.
"And us?" asked Arun.
Paati pointed to the last box, the thirty-first of December. "Humans like us come about half an hour before midnight, on the very last night of the year."
Arun was quiet for a moment. "So the tiny cells had the Earth nearly to themselves, almost all year?"
"Most of it," said Paati. "And they are still here, everywhere. In the sea, in the soil, even on your skin."
Kavya looked down at her arm. "Paati, if life began in water, where is my water?"
"Inside you," said Paati. "Every cell in your body is mostly water. That is where your own chemicals meet and react, all day and all night."
Kavya thought about the oil bowl. The powder had waited under the oil, ready, until the water reached it. She thought about the first cells in the old sea, and about the water inside her own hands.
Arun picked up the packet of fruit salt and held it tight in both hands. "I'll keep you dry," he told the packet, "until it's your turn."
story.epiphany: Kavya sees that the powders were ready all along, but could meet and change only in water. Life's chemicals also met in water, long ago, and her own cells still keep that water inside.

experiments.title: The Dry Mix: will the powders fizz without water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you mix two dry kitchen powders in four bowls. You keep one bowl dry and add oil, water or sea water to the others. Then you find out which ones change, and why.
experiments.question: Baking soda and citric acid sit together in a bowl. Do they change on their own, or only when we add a liquid? Which liquids make them change?
experiments.predict: We will mix the two dry powders in four bowls. One stays dry. One gets oil. One gets water. One gets salty water, as salty as the sea. Which bowls do you think will fizz? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every bowl gets the same powders: half a spoon of baking soda and half a spoon of citric acid. Every liquid is 2 spoons. A spoon always means a teaspoon here. The only thing we change is what we add. We watch each bowl for the same time, one minute, so no bowl gets longer to fizz.
results_table: My guess: fizz or no fizz?
experiments.safety: Citric acid stings if it gets in the eyes or a cut. Keep hands away from eyes, and if any powder gets in, rinse with plenty of water. Don't eat the powders by the spoonful.

materials.item: baking soda (also called cooking soda or meetha soda)
citric acid crystals, sold in grocery shops as nimbu sat or lemon salt. If you have none, use 4 teaspoons of fruit salt from a chemist, which already holds both powders.
4 small steel katoris or bowls, dry
a dry teaspoon
cooking oil
water in a tumbler
salt
4 paper slips and a pencil, to label the bowls

schedule.what: Make sea water. Put the dry mix in four bowls. Guess, then add oil, water and sea water. Then add water to the oil bowl and drip water on the dry bowl.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table for all four bowls. Draw each bowl: draw bubbles where you saw them. Then draw the oil bowl again after you added water.

flow.do: 1. Dry the four katoris well. 2. Label them dry, oil, water and sea water. 3. Stir 1 level spoon of salt into half a tumbler of water.
flow.say: We need sea water, but we live far from the beach. So let's make some. The sea is salty, about this salty.
flow.kid: Label four dry bowls. Stir one spoon of salt into half a tumbler of water. Taste one drop from your finger. That is how salty the sea is.
flow.parent: One level teaspoon of salt in about 150 millilitres of water is close to the saltiness of the sea. Keep a second, plain half tumbler of water ready too.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts half a spoon of baking soda and half a spoon of citric acid in each katori. 2. Wipe the spoon dry each time. 3. Stir each heap dry. 4. Look and listen.
flow.say: These two powders are now touching each other. Look closely. Put your ear near the bowl. Is anything happening?
flow.kid: Put half a spoon of each powder in every bowl. Stir them dry. Look closely. Listen. Is anything happening?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: The two powders look different. The crystals are bigger.

flow.parent: Nothing happens to the dry mix. This is the point of the test, so let your child notice it.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason for each bowl. Write the guesses in the table. Don't say what will happen.
flow.say: Now one bowl stays dry. One gets oil, one gets water and one gets sea water. Which ones do you think will fizz? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One bowl stays dry. The others get oil, water or sea water. Which will fizz? Say why. Write your guesses.

ask.q: Why do you think that one will fizz?
good: Oil is thick, so it will fizz more.

flow.parent: Many children guess that oil will fizz, or that salt will stop the fizz. Any guess with a reason is a good guess.

flow.do: 1. Pour 2 spoons of oil into the oil bowl. Watch for one minute. 2. Pour 2 spoons of water into the water bowl. Watch for one minute. 3. Pour 2 spoons of sea water into the sea water bowl. Watch for one minute. 4. Leave the dry bowl as it is.
flow.say: Let's do one bowl at a time and watch each one for a whole minute. What is happening in each bowl?
flow.kid: Pour oil into the oil bowl. Watch for one minute. Then do the water bowl. Then the sea water bowl. Write what happened.
flow.parent: The water and sea water bowls fizz at once and loudly. The oil bowl stays still, or shows only one or two bubbles. The dry bowl does nothing. If the oil bowl fizzes a lot, the powder or bowl was damp, so try again with a dry bowl.

flow.do: 1. Drip 2 spoons of plain water slowly into the oil bowl. 2. Watch where the drops go. 3. Then let one drop of water fall on the dry bowl.
flow.say: Was the powder in the oil bowl spoiled? Let's drip water into it and see. Then we put one single drop on the dry bowl.
flow.kid: Drip water into the oil bowl. Watch the drops sink. Then put one drop on the dry bowl. What happens?
flow.parent: Water is heavier than oil, so the drops sink to the powder. Bubbles then rise up through the oil. On the dry bowl, the fizz happens only where the drop lands.

flow.do: 1. Ask for the claim: what does your child now think? 2. Ask for the evidence: what did they see? 3. Ask for the reason: why? 4. Pour everything down the sink and rinse the bowls.
flow.say: Tell me what you think now. What did you see in each bowl? Why did only some of them fizz?
flow.kid: Say what you think now. Say what you saw in each bowl. Say why only some fizzed.

ask.q: Why did the powder in the oil fizz only when water reached it?
good: The powders need water to change.
The powder was ready all along. It only needed water.
Oil doesn't mix the powders, but water does.

flow.parent: A strong answer says the powders changed only when water reached them. Now read the card on why the powders fizzed only in water. It explains that water dissolves the powders, so their tiny pieces can meet and react.

check.q: In the oil bowl, the powder did not fizz until water reached it. What does this show?
options: The powders change only when water lets them meet
Oil spoils the powders for ever
The powders fizz on their own if you wait
check.why: When water reached the powder under the oil, it fizzed at once. So the powder was not spoiled. It needed water to react.

experiments.title: Sea Water Sprouts: can moong sprout in water as salty as the sea?
experiments.context: Life began in salty sea water, long ago. Moong plants live on land. In this experiment you find out whether moong seeds can sprout in water as salty as the sea.
experiments.question: Life began in the sea. Can moong seeds, from a plant that lives on land, sprout in water as salty as the sea?
experiments.predict: We will soak moong in plain water, in a little salty water, and in water as salty as the sea. In which cups do you think the moong will sprout? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Each cup gets 10 whole moong, the same amount of water and the same place in the room. The only thing we change is how much salt is in the water. We count every seed, because one seed on their own could be a fluke.

materials.item: whole green moong from the kitchen (sabut moong)
4 small cups or katoris (3 for the seeds, 1 for mixing)
a tumbler of water and a teaspoon
salt
3 paper slips and a pencil
3 small plates or lids, to cover the cups

schedule.what: Make three waters: plain, a little salty, and sea-salty. Put 10 moong in each cup. Cover the cups.
Count the moong that have a white root tip in each cup.
Count again. Compare the three cups and talk about what you found.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on day 2 and day 3. Draw one seed from each cup on day 3.

setup.art: Three small cups labelled plain, a little, and sea, each with a little water and ten green moong.
setup.caption: 1. Put 10 moong in each of three waters.

setup.art: The three cups covered with small steel plates on a kitchen shelf.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the cups and leave them.

setup.art: Day 3: moong with long white roots in the plain cup, and closed green seeds in the sea cup.
setup.caption: 3. Count the seeds with white root tips.

flow.do: 1. Label three cups: plain, a little, sea. 2. Stir 1 level spoon of salt into half a tumbler of water. This is sea-salty water. 3. Pour 4 spoons of sea-salty water into the sea cup. 4. In the fourth cup, mix 1 spoon of sea-salty water with 9 spoons of plain water. Pour 4 spoons of this into the cup labelled a little. 5. Pour 4 spoons of plain water into the plain cup. 6. Put 10 moong in each of the three cups and cover them.
flow.say: All life began in salty sea water, long ago. Moong plants live on land. Can their seeds sprout in sea water? What do you think? Why?
flow.kid: Label three cups: plain, a little, sea. Put sea-salty water in the sea cup. Put weak salty water in the a little cup. Put plain water in the plain cup. Put 10 moong in each cup. Cover them. Which will sprout? Say why.
flow.parent: Use fresh moong, because very old seeds may not sprout even in plain water. The weak salty water is about one tenth as salty as the sea. The seeds should sit in the water, not deep under it, so they get air too. Add a spoon of the same water if a cup dries out. Keep the cups on a warm shelf: in a cold room, sprouting is slow in every cup, so wait one more day before you count.
flow.wait: Leave the cups for one day

flow.do: 1. Lift the covers. 2. Your child counts the seeds with a white root tip showing in each cup. 3. Write the numbers. 4. Cover the cups again.
flow.say: A sprouted seed has a little white root poking out. Let's count them in each cup.
flow.kid: Look for a little white root on each seed. Count them in every cup. Write the numbers.
flow.parent: In a warm room, most seeds in plain water show a root by day 2. In sea-salty water most stay closed. They may swell a little, but few roots come out.
flow.wait: Leave the cups for one more day

flow.do: 1. Count again. 2. Compare the three cups. 3. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason.
flow.say: Which cup has the most sprouts? Which has the fewest? Life began in the sea, so why don't moong sprout well in sea water?
flow.kid: Count the sprouts again. Which cup has the most? Which has the fewest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why don't moong seeds sprout well in sea water?
good: Moong plants live on land, so they need fresh water.
Their family left the sea long ago.

flow.parent: Moong and their plant family have lived on land for hundreds of millions of years, with rain and river water. Over that long time, land plants changed, and most of them now need fresh water. Some plants still grow in salty water, such as the mangroves at Pichavaram in Tamil Nadu, Bhitarkanika in Odisha and the Sundarbans in West Bengal.

check.q: Most moong sprouted in plain water, and few sprouted in sea-salty water. What does this show?
options: Moong, a land plant, needs fresh water to sprout
check.why: Only the salt was different between the cups. The cup with sea-salty water had the fewest sprouts, so the salt stopped most of the moong.

activities.title: The Year of Life: the whole story on one calendar
activities.context: In this activity you squeeze the whole story of the Earth into one year. The Earth forms on 1 January, and today is midnight on 31 December. Then you find where the big moments of life go.

materials.item: an old wall calendar with a page for each month, or one sheet of paper with 12 boxes drawn on it, one for each month
crayons or colour pencils
12 small paper slips. A grown-up writes one event on each, from the list in step 2 (the 'Older Wins' cards work too)

schedule.what: Guess when life began. Then put the 12 events on the calendar and count the months of tiny cells.

activities.record: Keep the calendar with the 12 events on it. Colour the months that had only tiny cells in one colour.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with 12 boxes labelled January to December, and small paper slips beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Draw 12 boxes, one for each month.

setup.art: A child placing a slip with a small sea picture at the end of March, with most later months coloured pale blue.
setup.caption: 2. Put each event in its month.

setup.art: The December box crowded with tiny drawings of a dinosaur, a flower and a person in the last corner.
setup.caption: 3. Look how full December is.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the 12 months. 2. Explain the game. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Let's pretend the whole story of the Earth is one year. The Earth forms on the first of January. Right now is midnight on the thirty-first of December. In which month do you think the first living beings came? Why?
flow.kid: The whole story of the Earth is one year. The Earth forms on 1 January. Now is midnight on 31 December. When did life begin? Point to a month.
flow.parent: Write down the guess. Many children guess the middle of the year, or December. The real answer surprises most grown-ups too.

flow.do: Read each event slip aloud, one at a time. Your child puts each one in the right month. 1 January, the Earth forms. About 9 January, the first oceans. End of March, the first signs of tiny cells, in stromatolites. Late June, tiny cells have put the first oxygen into the air. Mid-November, the first animals big enough to see, soft and flat, in the sea. About 18 November, sea animals with shells, eyes and legs, and soon the first fish. About 24 November, the first small plants on land. About 1 December, the first animals with four legs walk onto land. About 13 December, the first dinosaurs. About 21 December, the first flowers. 26 December, a huge rock from space hits the Earth, and most dinosaurs die out, but birds live on. 31 December, about half an hour before midnight, the first humans like us, in Africa.
flow.say: Let's put each moment in its month. Watch what happens to the calendar as we go.
flow.kid: Listen to each event. Put the slip in the right month. Watch which months fill up.
flow.parent: On this calendar, one day stands for about 12 million years. The dates are rounded. Scientists still argue a little about some of them, for example when the very first cells began.

flow.do: 1. Colour the months from April to October in one colour: tiny cells only. 2. Count them together. 3. Ask what your child notices.
flow.say: Let's colour every month that had only tiny cells, too small to see. How many months is that? What do you notice about December?
flow.kid: Colour April to October. Count the months. Then look at December. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice about the calendar now?
good: Most of the year is only tiny cells.
Everything big comes in November and December.
Humans come right at the very end.

flow.parent: From the end of March to the middle of November is more than 7 months of tiny cells. Some many-celled seaweeds lived before November too, but almost all life was tiny cells.

check.q: On the Year of Life calendar, what lived on Earth from April to October?
options: Almost only tiny cells, too small to see
check.why: The first big animals come in the middle of November. Before that, almost all life was tiny cells in water.

activities.title: How Small Was the First Life? A hair and a dot
activities.context: This short activity helps you picture how small the first living beings were. You look at one hair and a pencil dot, and compare them with a tiny cell.

materials.item: one hair from a comb
a sheet of white paper
a sharp pencil
a magnifying glass, or a phone camera that can zoom in, if you have one

schedule.what: Look at a hair and a pencil dot, then picture 50 tiny cells across the hair.

activities.record: Draw the hair very big across your page. Draw a row of tiny circles across its width, as many as you can fit.

setup.art: A single dark hair lying across a sheet of white paper next to a small pencil dot.
setup.caption: 1. Lay one hair on white paper.

setup.art: A hair drawn huge, with a row of about 50 tiny circles across its width.
setup.caption: 2. Picture 50 tiny cells across the hair.

flow.do: 1. Lay the hair on the white paper. 2. Make the smallest dot you can beside it. 3. Look at both, with a magnifying glass if you have one.
flow.say: This hair is very thin. Can you see how wide it is? Now make the smallest dot you can. Which is thinner?
flow.kid: Put the hair on white paper. Make a tiny dot beside it. Which is thinner, the hair or the dot?

flow.do: 1. Tell your child how small the first cells were. 2. Your child draws the hair very big, with tiny circles across it.
flow.say: The first living beings were tiny cells. Tiny cells today are so small that about 50 of them, side by side, would just stretch across this one hair. How could anyone find something so small, from so long ago?
flow.kid: About 50 tiny cells fit across one hair. Draw the hair very big. Draw tiny cells across it.
flow.parent: Scientists find the first life in two ways: stromatolites, the layered rocks that mats of cells built, and tiny fossil cells seen with powerful microscopes.

check.q: How big were the first living beings?
options: Far too small to see, about 50 across one hair
check.why: The first living beings were single cells, as tiny as the cells of bacteria today. About 50 of those, side by side, fit across one hair.

activities.title: Sea Cousins at the Fish Market (if your family buys fish or seafood)
activities.context: Many kinds of living beings still live in the sea, where life began. In this activity you look closely at sea animals at a fish market or in your kitchen, and count the legs of a crab and find eyes.

materials.item: a visit to a fish market, or seafood your family has bought, such as prawns, a crab, squid or a whole fish
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Look at sea animals at the market or in the kitchen. Count the kinds, and count the legs and find the eyes of two of them.

activities.record: Draw two sea animals. Write how many legs the crab has and where the eyes are. Write how many different kinds you saw.

setup.art: A fish market stall in Kochi with prawns, crabs, squid and silver fish laid out on ice.
setup.caption: 1. Count how many kinds you see.

setup.art: A child counting the legs of a crab on a steel plate in a kitchen.
setup.caption: 2. Count a crab's legs and find the eyes of two animals.

flow.do: 1. Walk along the stalls, or lay out the seafood on a plate. 2. Count how many different kinds of animals you see.
flow.say: All of these animals came from the sea. Let's count how many different kinds there are.
flow.kid: Look at all the sea animals. Count how many kinds you can see.
flow.parent: Families who don't eat fish can do this with pictures in a book, or skip it. Ask before touching anything at a stall.

flow.do: 1. Pick a crab or a prawn, and one other animal. 2. Count the crab's legs and find the eyes of both. 3. Your child draws them.
flow.say: Count this crab's legs. Can you find the eyes? Now look at the other animal. Long ago, the sea had animals called trilobites, with shells and many legs, a bit like a crab.
flow.kid: Count the crab's legs. Find the eyes of both animals. Draw them.
flow.parent: A crab has 8 legs for walking and 2 claws. Crabs and prawns are arthropods, animals with jointed legs and a hard outer shell. Trilobites were arthropods too. They lived in the sea for about 270 million years and then died out.

games.title: Older Wins: a card game about the story of life
games.players: 2 players, or 1 child with a grown-up
games.context: This is a card game about the order of the story of life. Each player turns over a card, and the event that happened first wins both cards.

printables.title: 12 event cards, with the Year of Life date on the back

items.f: The Earth forms, hot and rocky.
items.b: 1 January on the Year of Life. About 4.5 billion years ago.
About 9 January. About 4.4 billion years ago.

items.f: The first signs of tiny cells, in stromatolites.
items.b: End of March. About 3.5 billion years ago.

items.f: Tiny cells put the first oxygen into the air.
items.b: Late June. About 2.4 billion years ago.

items.f: The first animals big enough to see, soft and flat, in the sea.
Sea animals with shells, eyes and legs.
items.b: About 18 November. About 540 million years ago.

items.f: The first small plants on land.
items.b: About 24 November. About 470 million years ago.

items.f: The first animals with four legs walk onto land.
items.b: About 1 December. About 375 million years ago.
About 13 December. About 230 million years ago.
About 21 December. About 130 million years ago.

items.f: A huge rock from space hits the Earth. Most dinosaurs die out, but birds live on.
The first humans like us, in Africa.
items.b: 31 December, half an hour before midnight. About 300,000 years ago.

rules: Mix the cards. Deal 6 cards to each player, face down in a pile.
Both players turn over their top card at the same time and read it aloud.
Each player says which event they think happened first, and why.
Turn both cards over to check the dates on the back. The event that happened first, the older one, wins. Its player keeps both cards.
Play until the piles run out. The player with the most cards wins. If you both have 6 cards, you both win.

setup.art: Twelve event cards dealt into two face-down piles on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Deal 6 cards each, face down.

setup.art: Two children each turning over a card: one shows sea animals with shells, the other the first dinosaurs.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over one card each. The older event wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Mix them and deal 6 cards each, face down.
flow.say: Each card is a moment in the story of life. The date is on the back, but don't peek until we have both guessed.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Don't look at the backs.

flow.do: 1. Play as the rules say. 2. Each time, ask why that event came first before turning the cards over.
flow.say: Your card says sea animals with shells and mine says the first dinosaurs. Which came first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Turn over your top card. Read it out. Which event came first? Say why. Then check the backs.
flow.parent: A good reason uses the story: animals lived in the sea before they walked on land, and tiny cells came before everything big.

flow.do: 1. Lay all 12 cards in a line, oldest first. 2. Ask what your child notices.
flow.say: Let's put all the cards in a line, the oldest first. Where do most of the big animals come?
flow.kid: Put all the cards in a line, oldest first. Where are most of the big animals?

check.q: Which of these came first in the story of life?
options: The first animals with four legs on land
Sea animals with shells, eyes and legs
check.why: Animals with shells, eyes and legs lived in the sea about 540 million years ago. Four-legged animals walked onto land about 375 million years ago, and flowers came about 130 million years ago.

games.title: One Becomes Many: the splitting game
games.context: This is a dice game about how one tiny cell becomes many. Each player starts with one chana, which stands for one cell. When a cell gets food, the cell splits in two.

printables.title: Score sheet: print one for each player
items: Turn 1: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 2: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 3: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 4: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 5: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 6: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 7: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 8: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 9: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 10: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 11: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 12: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 13: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 14: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___
Turn 15: I rolled ___. Food or no food? ___. My cells now: ___

rules: Each player has a katori with 1 chana (a dried chickpea) in it. That chana is your first cell.
Put a bowl with about 150 more chana in the middle.
You need a dice. If you have none, write 1 to 6 on six paper slips and pick one from a cup.
On your turn, roll the dice. An even number, 2, 4 or 6, means food: every one of your cells splits in two. Double your chana.
An odd number, 1, 3 or 5, means no food this time. Your cells stay as they are.
Count your cells out loud and write the number on your score sheet. If the game goes past 15 turns, write on the back.
The first player to reach 32 cells wins. Finish the round. If two or more players reach 32 in the same round, they all win.

setup.art: Four steel katoris, each with one chana in it, a dice and a bowl of chana in the middle.
setup.caption: 1. Start with 1 chana each: your first cell.

setup.art: A child doubling a heap of 4 chana to make 8, after rolling a 6.
setup.caption: 2. Even number: every cell splits. Double them.

flow.do: 1. Give each player a katori with 1 chana. 2. Put a bowl of chana in the middle. 3. Read the rules together.
flow.say: This chana is a tiny cell in the old sea. When a cell gets food, they grow and split into two cells. Let's see how fast one becomes many.
flow.kid: Your chana is one tiny cell. Food makes a cell split in two. Read the rules.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling. 2. Double the chana on an even number. 3. Count aloud and fill in the score sheet.
flow.say: You rolled a 4, so your cells got food. Every cell splits. You had 4, so how many now?
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Even number? Double your chana. Count them out loud. Write the number.
flow.parent: The numbers go 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. Real tiny cells split like this when they have plenty of food. Some can split every 20 minutes.

flow.do: Ask what your child noticed about how the numbers grew.
flow.say: At first you had only 1 or 2 cells. How fast did they grow at the end? Why?
flow.kid: Look at your score sheet. Did your cells grow faster at the end? Why?

check.q: In the splitting game, you have 8 cells and every one splits in two. How many cells do you have now?
check.why: Every one of the 8 cells becomes 2 cells, so you have 8 and 8 more, which is 16. Adding just one cell gives 9, but here every cell splits.

projects.title: A Shoebox Sea from Long Ago
projects.context: In this two-day project you make a model of the sea more than 500 million years ago, when the first animals big enough to see lived there. You make the animals from dough and paper.

materials.item: a shoebox or any small cardboard box
crayons, paints or blue paper for the sea
a ball of atta dough, made with a little salt so it keeps, or clay
green paper or old green ribbon, for seaweed
thread and sticky tape
small paper slips for labels

schedule.what: Colour the inside of the box like the sea. Make seaweed from green paper and dome-shaped stromatolites from dough.
Make four or five strange sea animals from dough. Hang some on threads. Label each one.

projects.record: Take a photo of your shoebox sea, or draw it. Write the name of each animal on a label.

setup.art: A shoebox on its side, coloured blue inside, with paper seaweed and dough domes on the floor.
setup.caption: 1. Make the sea, the seaweed and the stromatolites.

setup.art: Dough animals in the box: a flat oval with ridges, a fern-shaped frond, a trilobite and a five-eyed Opabinia hanging on a thread.
setup.caption: 2. Add the strange sea animals.

flow.do: 1. Stand the box on its side. 2. Colour the inside blue, like the sea. 3. Cut seaweed strips from green paper and tape them to the floor. 4. Make three dough domes for stromatolites.
flow.say: This is the sea long ago. No plants or animals lived on land yet. The domes are stromatolites, built by mats of tiny cells.
flow.kid: Colour the inside of the box blue. Make seaweed from green paper. Make three dough domes. These are stromatolites.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child about the animals in the parent note. 2. Your child picks four or five and makes them from dough. 3. Hang one or two on threads, as if swimming.
flow.say: Long ago the sea had animals that look strange to us. One had five eyes. One was flat like a mat. Which ones will you make?
flow.kid: Pick four or five sea animals from long ago. Make them from dough. Hang one on a thread, swimming.
flow.parent: Real animals to make: Dickinsonia, flat and oval with ridges across, with no head and no legs. Charnia, shaped like a fern leaf, fixed to the sea floor. A trilobite, with a hard shell, many legs and eyes. Opabinia, with five eyes and a long nose with a claw at the end. Hallucigenia, with spikes on the back and soft legs underneath. They did not all live at the same time, but all of them lived more than 500 million years ago.

flow.do: 1. Label each animal. 2. Ask your child to show the box to someone and tell them about it.
flow.say: Tell someone at home about your sea. Which animal is your favourite? How is that animal different from animals today?
flow.kid: Write a label for each animal. Show your sea to someone. Tell them about your favourite animal.

challenges.title: Fizz Later: make the powder wait in water
challenges.context: In the dry mix test, the powders fizzed as soon as water reached them. This challenge asks you to make a little packet that waits in water before it fizzes.
challenges.problem: Make a small packet of the dry mix that you drop into a tumbler of water. It should wait as long as you can before it starts to fizz, and then it must still fizz. Aim for at least 5 seconds.
constraints: Use only half a spoon of baking soda and half a spoon of citric acid.
Use only home things: tissue, paper, thread, a little cooking oil, sticky tape.
Drop the packet into a tumbler of water, and count the seconds until the first bubbles.
The packet must fizz in the end.
materials: tissue paper or a paper napkin
general: Wrap the mix in one layer of tissue and twist the top. The water takes a second or two to soak through.
Wrap it in two or three layers, so the water takes even longer to reach the powder.
creative: Mix the powders with a few drops of oil, then wrap the mix. The oil may slow the water down. It may also make the fizz small, and that is a result too.
Use thicker paper, like newspaper, folded into a tiny envelope.
challenges.your_turn: Design your own packet. Drop it in and count the seconds. Then change one thing and try again. Which packet waited longest and still fizzed?

setup.art: A small twist of tissue paper with white powder inside, held over a steel tumbler of water.
setup.caption: 1. Wrap the dry mix in a packet.

setup.art: The tissue packet floating in the tumbler, with the first bubbles starting through the paper.
setup.caption: 2. Drop it in. Count the seconds to the first bubbles.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask why the powders fizzed so fast in the test. 3. Ask for ideas before showing any.
flow.say: The powders fizzed the moment water reached them. How could we slow the water down, so the packet waits before it fizzes?
flow.kid: The powders fizz when water reaches them. How can you slow the water down? Think of ideas.

flow.do: Your child makes a first packet from their own idea.
flow.say: Make your first packet. What do you think will happen when it goes in the water?
flow.kid: Make your first packet. Guess how many seconds it will wait.

flow.do: 1. Drop the packet in. 2. Count the seconds aloud until the first bubbles. 3. Write the number. 4. Try a second design.
flow.say: Drop it in. Let's count together: one, two, three. When do the bubbles start?
flow.kid: Drop it in. Count the seconds until the bubbles start. Write the number. Try another packet.
flow.parent: One layer of tissue often waits only a second or two. Three layers, or folded newspaper taped shut, usually wait longer. Results differ from home to home. If no packet reaches 5 seconds, the one that waited longest wins.

flow.do: Compare the packets and ask which worked best, and why.
flow.say: Which packet waited the longest? Why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which packet waited the longest? Why did it work?

check.q: A packet with three layers of tissue waited longer than a packet with one layer. Why?
options: The water took longer to reach the powder
The tissue made the powders weaker
check.why: The powders react only when water reaches them. More layers meant the water took longer to soak through.

items.p: In the dry mix test, which of these bowls fizzed as soon as you added the liquid?
items.why: Water dissolved the powders, so they could meet and react. Picking the oil bowl may mean thinking any liquid works, but oil does not dissolve these powders.
items.context: This question is about the dry mix test. You mixed baking soda and citric acid in four bowls, and added nothing, oil, water or sea water.

items.p: Draw the water bowl just after you added the water. Show where the bubbles were.
items.a: A katori with powder and water, and bubbles rising all over it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows many bubbles where the water touched the powder, as in the child's own test.
items.context: This question is about the dry mix test. You mixed baking soda and citric acid in four bowls, and added nothing, oil, water or sea water.

items.p: Sea water made the dry mix fizz too.
items.why: True. Sea water is water with salt in it. The water still dissolved the powders, so they fizzed.
items.context: This question is about the dry mix test. You mixed baking soda and citric acid in four bowls, and added nothing, oil, water or sea water.

items.p: Draw a line from each word to what it means.
pairs: the smallest part of a living being that is alive by itself
the mark of a living being from long ago, kept in rock
when chemicals meet and change into new ones
a line that shows things in the order they happened
items.why: These are the four words the child needs most in this unit.

items.p: Why do scientists say life began in water?
opts: The chemicals of life can move about, meet and react in water
Water is cold and keeps things asleep
There was no land at all
items.why: Just as the powders met and fizzed only in water, the chemicals of life met and changed in water. There was land, but life began in the sea.
items.context: This question is about where life began, which you read about after the dry mix test.

items.p: The first living beings on Earth lived in ____.
items.why: The chemicals of life meet and react in water, and the oldest signs of life come from rocks that formed in sea water.

items.p: Three of these need water inside them to stay alive. Which one does not?
items.why: A steel spoon is not alive. Every living being, in water or on land, has cells that are mostly water inside.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Kochi, and her friend Farhan, a boy in Class 2, look at the oil bowl before any water was added.

views.says: The oil spoiled the powder, so it can never fizz.
The powder is not spoiled. It just has no water.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason from your own test. Then say one thing the other person noticed that is true.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Lakshmi, because the powder fizzed under the oil once water reached it. It also says Farhan was right that nothing happened while there was only oil.
items.why: The test answers this: water dripped into the oil bowl made it fizz. Farhan's observation was true, but his reason was not.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: a moong seed can stay dry for months. What do you think a moong seed needs, to begin to grow?
items.a: Water. The seed is alive but waiting, and starts to grow when water reaches the seed.
items.why: A strong answer says the seed needs water to start growing, like the first cells needed water.

items.p: Label the four bowls from the dry mix test: dry, oil, water, sea water. Then draw bubbles in the bowls that fizzed.
items.why: Only the bowls with water in them fizzed.

items.p: Put these moments in the story of life in order, the oldest first.
items: The first animals big enough to see
items.why: Tiny cells came about 3.5 billion years ago, big animals about 575 million, dinosaurs about 230 million, and humans only about 300,000 years ago.
items.context: This question is about the Year of Life calendar, where the whole story of the Earth is squeezed into one year, from 1 January to 31 December.

items.p: Sort these living beings: lives in water, or lives on land.
items.why: Many kinds still live in water, where all life began. The land kinds came from ancestors who once lived in water.

items.p: Tiny cells like the first living cells are very small. About how many would fit side by side across one hair?
items.why: Tiny cells like the first cells are far too small to see. About 50 of them, side by side, would just stretch across one hair.
items.context: This question is about the hair and the first cells, from the activity on how small the first life was.

items.p: The first living beings had no bones and no shells. Why do you think their fossils are layered rocks called stromatolites, and not bones?
items.a: Because they were tiny soft cells. The only thing big enough to stay was the layered rock their mats built.
items.why: A strong answer says tiny cells leave no bones, so we find the rocks their mats built, layer by layer.

items.p: Draw a stromatolite cut in half, with its layers. Draw the mat of tiny cells on top, in the shallow sea.
items.a: A dome of wavy layers, with a thin living layer on top and water above it.
items.why: A strong drawing shows many thin layers, one on top of another, with the living mat only on the very top.

items.p: Humans and the big dinosaurs lived at the same time.
items.why: False. Most dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago, on 26 December on the Year of Life. Humans came about 300,000 years ago, on the last night. Birds are the dinosaurs who lived on.

items.p: On the Year of Life calendar, the first flowers came on about 21 December. Humans came on 31 December. How many days are there from 21 December to 31 December?
items.why: 31 take away 21 is 10. So flowers had been around for 10 days of the calendar before humans came.
items.context: This question is about the Year of Life calendar, where the whole story of the Earth is squeezed into one year, from 1 January to 31 December.

views.says: Life is mostly big plants and animals, like trees and elephants.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use the Year of Life calendar as your evidence. Then say what the other person could answer back.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence, for example that tiny cells had almost all of the year to themselves. It also gives the other side's best point: by weight, trees and other plants make up most of the living things on Earth today.
items.why: Both have a point. By time, and by numbers, life is mostly tiny cells. By weight, most living matter today is plants. Scientists measured this in 2018.
items.context: This question is about the Year of Life calendar, where the whole story of the Earth is squeezed into one year, from 1 January to 31 December.

items.why: Most of the year is tiny cells. Everything big is crowded into November and December.

items.p: Many people think the first living beings were fish. What evidence shows they were not?
items.a: The oldest fossils are stromatolites and tiny cells, about 3.5 billion years old. Fish fossils appear only about 500 million years ago.
items.why: A strong answer uses the order of fossils in the rocks: tiny cells come far earlier than any fish.

items.p: In 1862, Lord Kelvin said the Earth was much younger than it is. What did he not know about?
opts: Radioactive rock, which heats the Earth from inside
items.why: Radioactivity was found only in 1896. It heats the Earth, so the Earth cooled much more slowly than Kelvin worked out. People already knew the Earth was round.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Madurai, and Rukhsana, a girl in Srinagar, are arguing about where life began.

views.says: Life began at hot springs on the deep sea floor, where warm water is full of chemicals.
Life began in warm pools on land, which dried out and filled up again.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Give one reason. Then say what the other person might answer back. Is there a way scientists could find out?
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'drying pushes chemicals close together', and gives the other side's reason too. It may say that nobody knows yet, and that scientists test both ideas in labs.
items.why: This is a real argument among scientists. Both ideas have some evidence, and the question is still open.

items.p: Draw what you think the very first living cell looked like, floating in water. Label its thin skin and its watery inside.
items.a: A tiny round cell with a thin skin and a watery inside, floating in water.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a skin around a watery inside, floating in water.

items.p: When living beings moved from the water onto land, they left all their water behind.
items.why: False. Every land plant and animal still has cells that are mostly water inside. More than half of your body is water.

items.p: Monkeys slowly turned into humans.
items.why: False. Monkeys and humans are cousins. They both come from the same ancestors, who lived millions of years ago and were neither.

items.p: Predict: if you added each of these liquids to the dry mix, would it fizz or not? Sort them.
items.why: Milk, lemon juice and tender coconut water are mostly water, so they dissolve the powders. Coconut oil and ghee are fats, like cooking oil, so they do not.

items.p: A friend says a packet of fruit salt is broken, because it has sat on the shelf for a year and never fizzed. What would you tell them? How could you test it?
items.a: It is not broken. It is dry, so the powders cannot meet. Put a pinch in water and it will fizz.
items.why: A strong answer explains that the powders need water to react, and suggests a fair test: a pinch in water.

items.p: A tiny cell with plenty of food splits in two every 20 minutes. You start with 1 cell. How many cells are there after one hour?
items.why: One hour is three lots of 20 minutes. 1 becomes 2, then 4, then 8.

items.p: The first animals big enough to see appeared only in November on the Year of Life. What do scientists think is one reason it took so long?
opts: The sea and the air had very little oxygen for a long time
The Sun was not shining yet
There was no water until November
items.why: Many scientists think big animals needed more oxygen, and oxygen built up slowly. They still argue about the other reasons. The Sun and the oceans were there from the start.

quiz.p: Why did the fruit salt in the packet not fizz for months?
opts: It was dry, so the powders could not meet
quiz.why: The powders react only when water dissolves them. Picking 'too old' may mean thinking the powder went bad, but a pinch in water still fizzes.

quiz.p: Where did life on Earth begin?
quiz.why: The chemicals of life meet and react in water, and the oldest signs of life come from rocks made in sea water.

quiz.p: What is most of every cell in your body made of?
quiz.why: Every cell is mostly water inside. That is where the body's chemicals meet and react.

quiz.p: What were the first living beings like?
opts: Tiny cells, far too small to see
quiz.why: The first life was single tiny cells. Fish and dinosaurs came billions of years later.

opts: A rock built in layers by mats of tiny cells
quiz.why: Mats of tiny cells in shallow water trap sand, then grow up through it, again and again. That builds a layered rock.

quiz.p: Which of these came first in the story of life: tiny cells, fish or dinosaurs?
quiz.why: Tiny cells came about 3.5 billion years ago. Fish came about 500 million years ago, and dinosaurs about 230 million.

quiz.p: Which of these came last: humans, flowers or dinosaurs?
quiz.why: Humans like us came only about 300,000 years ago. Flowers came about 130 million years ago, and dinosaurs before that.

quiz.p: If the story of the Earth were one year, when would humans like us appear?
opts: About half an hour before midnight on 31 December
quiz.why: On the Year of Life, one day is about 12 million years. 300,000 years is only about half an hour.

quiz.p: Where do all the living beings alive today come from?
opts: From the first cells, through a very long line of parents
Each kind appeared suddenly, all at once
quiz.why: Every living being comes from parents, and they from theirs, all the way back to the first cells.

quiz.p: How did a few kinds of tiny cells become so many kinds of living beings?
opts: Small changes added up over a very, very long time
They all changed in one day
quiz.why: Children are a little different from their parents. Over thousands and thousands of generations, these small differences add up into new kinds.

applications: Fizzy powders like fruit salt are packed in dry, sealed sachets, so they wait until they meet water.

Many medicines are kept in sealed strips, because damp air can make them change before you need them.

open_questions.q: How exactly did the first living cell begin?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made some of life's chemicals in labs, and even RNA chains that help join other chains. Nobody has yet made a living cell from chemicals.

open_questions.q: Where did life begin: at hot springs in the deep sea, in warm pools on land, or somewhere else?

open_questions.why_open: Nobody has looked there yet. Space missions are now being sent to find out more about these oceans.

maths.problem: On the Year of Life calendar, the first signs of tiny cells come at the end of March. The first animals big enough to see come in the middle of November. Name the months in between, from April to October. How many months is that?
maths.answer: April, May, June, July, August, September and October: 7 months. So for more than 7 months of the year, almost all life was tiny cells.
maths.explain: Count the months on your fingers, starting with April: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. The ends of March and the start of November add a little more.
maths.context: This question is about the Year of Life calendar, where the whole story of the Earth is squeezed into one year.
maths.why_maths: Counting the months shows how long tiny cells had the Earth almost to themselves.

maths.problem: In the splitting game, Lakshmi, a girl in Kochi, starts with 1 cell. Every time she rolls an even number, every cell splits in two. How many cells does she have after 1 split, 2 splits, 3 splits, 4 splits and 5 splits? What pattern do you see?
maths.answer: 2, 4, 8, 16 and 32. Each time, the number doubles.
maths.explain: 1 and 1 more is 2. 2 and 2 is 4. 4 and 4 is 8. 8 and 8 is 16. 16 and 16 is 32. Each number is the last one added to itself.
maths.context: This question is about the splitting game, where each chana stands for one tiny cell that splits in two when they get food.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the doubling pattern lets you predict how fast one cell becomes many, without counting every chana.

maths.problem: Nandini, a girl in Bengaluru, did the dry mix test in 3 bowls with water and 3 bowls with oil. Her tally of bowls that fizzed: water |||, oil none. Then she dripped water into the 3 oil bowls, and all of them fizzed. How many bowls fizzed in the end? What does that tell her?
maths.answer: 6 bowls fizzed in the end: 3 and 3. It tells her the powder under the oil was ready all along. It only needed water.
maths.explain: 3 water bowls fizzed first. Then 3 more fizzed when water reached them. 3 + 3 = 6.
maths.context: This question is about the dry mix test. You mixed baking soda and citric acid in bowls, and added nothing, oil, water or sea water.
maths.why_maths: A tally before and after the water shows at a glance that only the water made a difference.

maths.problem: In the sea water sprouts test, Bidisha, a girl in Kolkata, put 10 moong in plain water and 10 in sea-salty water. 9 sprouted in plain water and 1 sprouted in sea-salty water. How many more sprouted in plain water?
maths.explain: 9 take away 1 is 8. The difference is big, so the salt clearly made a difference, not chance.
maths.context: This question is about the sea water sprouts test. You soaked moong in plain water, in a little salty water, and in water as salty as the sea.
maths.why_maths: Finding the difference shows how big the effect of the salt was, so we can tell whether it is a real result or a fluke.

roots.context: We found that dry powders change only when water lets them meet, and we squeezed the story of life into one year. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Dry soda and citric acid sat together and did nothing. A few drops of water made them fizz at once. Inside every cell, chemicals are dissolved in water, so they can meet and react. That is why scientists say life began in water, and why your cells are still mostly water.
deep_truth.habit: We think of water as something we drink, and of the sea as a faraway place. But water is where the chemistry of every living being happens. When plants and animals moved onto land, they took water with them, inside every cell.
deep_truth.evidence: In the dry mix test, the dry bowl and the oil bowl did not fizz. The water and sea water bowls fizzed at once, and the oil bowl fizzed as soon as water reached the powder. The oldest signs of life, stromatolites about 3.5 billion years old, formed in shallow sea water.

three.who_am_i: You are mostly water. Each of your cells keeps water inside, where your body's chemicals meet and react.
three.what_is_life: Life began as tiny cells in water. Everything alive today, from a crow to a coconut tree to you, comes from those first cells.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth was here a very long time before anything big enough to see lived on it. For most of the story, its life was tiny cells.

roots.thread: Before life, the young Earth had rock, water and chemicals, and no living being anywhere. In the water, chemicals met and changed, again and again. Then came the first living cells, and from those few came every kind of being, first in the sea and later on land. Everything is conscious, the smallest cells too: tiny cells today sense food and swim towards it, and the first cells sensed their world as well. One beginning in water became all the life there is now.

teachings.source: Rig Veda 10.129.3 (the Nasadiya Sukta, the hymn of creation)
teachings.teaching: In the beginning, darkness was hidden by darkness. All this was water, with nothing to tell one thing from another.
teachings.link: The old hymn pictures the beginning as water. Science also finds that life began in water. The same hymn later asks who really knows how it all began. Scientists still ask that about the first cell.

teachings.teaching: From space came air. From air came fire, from fire water, and from water the earth. From the earth came plants, from plants food, and from food the person.
teachings.link: This is a story of beginnings in order, like the Year of Life calendar. The order science finds is different in places: the rocky Earth came before the oceans. But both put a person at the end of a long line that runs through water and plants.

teachings.source: Thales of Miletus, as told by Aristotle in Metaphysics, Book 1, chapter 3
teachings.teaching: Thales, a Greek thinker, said that water is where all things come from. Aristotle guessed Thales thought this because food and seeds are always moist.
teachings.link: Thales was wrong that everything is made of water. But he noticed something true: living things need water, and life did begin in it.

science.text: Life began in water more than 3.5 billion years ago, and every living being today comes from the first cells.
Exactly where in the water life began, and how the first cell formed, is still unknown.

other_view.view: They say life began from chemistry and chance alone. In their view, the first cells and the chemicals before them had no awareness. Awareness came much later, with brains.

practice.title: One slow sip
practice.say: Pour a little water into a tumbler. Look at the water for a moment. Now take one slow sip. Feel it cool in your mouth, then going down. Close your eyes and breathe slowly, three times. Soon this water will be inside your cells. Life began in water like this, long ago. Now open your eyes.
